A.biggest_strength: Interactive multi-step gradient descent training loop ('Take a gradient step' with learning rate selection and live loss sparkline) combined with click-to-trace chain-rule paths and a live finite-difference gradient check table.
A.biggest_weakness: The computation graph relies on text-heavy boxes without geometric visualizations of the activation/loss derivatives, and its 820px min-width SVG is clipped horizontally on mobile screens.

B.biggest_strength: True visual explanations of the mathematical mechanisms—separating linear and activation nodes in the graph, plotting tangent slopes on the loss and sigmoid curves, showing outer-product weight gradient matrices, and adapting to a dedicated vertical graph layout on mobile.
B.biggest_weakness: In the Scene 4 sigmoid plot, the 'slope 0.235' label collides with the curve and tangent line, and the Update scene only previews a single gradient step from the initial weights rather than allowing iterative multi-step training.

structured_output.reasons: Both pages are mathematically accurate and well-crafted for a machine learning course, with zero factual errors. Page B wins because it visually explains the underlying calculus and linear algebra mechanisms—splitting pre-activation (z) and activation (h) into separate graph nodes, plotting live tangent slopes on the loss and sigmoid curves, visualizing the outer-product matrix structure of weight gradients, showing fan-out gradient summation at the inputs, and reflowing the entire computation graph into a vertical top-to-bottom layout that fits cleanly on a phone screen. Page A excels in its interactive multi-step gradient descent button and click-to-trace parameter paths, but its visual representation is mostly text lines inside boxes and overflows horizontally on mobile.
